s: Toronto (the capital city of Ontario, Canada and the largest city in Canada)
gate, archway (passageway covered by an arch, particularly one made of masonry)
gate, door (large doorway, opening, or passage in a fence or wall)
Dies ist ein Garagentor, nur ein Ochse parkt davor.
This is a garage door, only an ox parks in front of it.
gateway (point that represents the beginning of a transition from one place or phase to another)
Cham, das Tor zum Bayerwald - Cham, the gateway to the Bavarian Forest
goal, net (area into which the players attempt to put a ball)
goal (The act of scoring a goal in sports where doing so is the object)
Tor.et: From Middle High German and Old High German tor, from Proto-West Germanic *dor, from Proto-Germanic *durą.

s: fool (person with poor judgment or little intelligence)
Fuͤrwahr! er dient euch auf beſondre Weiſe. / Nicht irdiſch iſt des Thoren Trank noch Speiſe.
Indeed! He serves you in a peculiar way. The drink and food of fools is not of this earth.
2nd half of the 18th century, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Prometheus (transl. "Prometheus")
Your majesty / Is barely nourished / By sacrificial offerings / And prayerful exhalations, / And should starve / Were children and beggars not / Fools full of Hope.
Tor.et: From Middle High German tōre (literally “hazy, foggy”), from the root of Dunst (“haze”). Cognate with Swedish dåre (from Low German).

Tornado.et: Borrowed from Spanish tornado in the 19th century, from English tornado, from Spanish tronada.

Torpedo.et: Borrowed from English torpedo, from Latin.

s: a typically multilayered, often round cake with fillings of all kinds, often with icing and garnish
Torte.et: 15th century, from Middle French tarte, tourte, later reinforced by Italian torta, all from Late Latin torta (“cake, round loaf”).

s: eleventh hour panic (the fear that time to act is running out)
Die Torschlusspanik der Midlife-Krise hat schon manchen gesetzten Herren in die Arme einer Jüngeren getrieben und damit viele Ehen zerstört.
Midlife-crisis-induced Torschlusspanik has driven quite a few middle-aged men into the arms of young women, wrecking countless marriages.
Torschlusspanik.et: From Tor + Schluss + Panik, literally “gate-shut panic”. For safety reasons city gates used to be shut at nightfall (Torschluss, from Tor + Schluss), leaving latecomers no other choice than to stay outside, thereby exposing them to various dangers.

Torf.et: From Middle Low German torf, from Old Saxon turf, *torf, from Proto-West Germanic *turb, from Proto-Germanic *turbz, from Proto-Indo-European *derbʰ-. The Proto-Germanic etymon was possibly inherited in Old High German as zurf (one attestation). More at turf.

s: the sound of a trumpeting elephant
törö.et: Onomatopoeic. Popularized by the children’s audio drama series Benjamin Blümchen (since 1977).

Torwart.et: Formally from Middle High German torwart, torwarte (“doorkeeper, gatekeeper”), from Old High German torwart, torwarto (“doorkeeper, porter”). By surface analysis, Tor (“goal”) + Wart (“guardian”).

s: a male given name from Danish, popular in the 1960s and 1970s
Torsten.et: From Danish Torsten, from Old Norse Þorsteinn, the root of English Thurstan, from Þórr (“Thor”) + steinn (“stone”).

s: a male given name recently borrowed from Danish Torben; variant form Thorben

Torkel.et: Old High German torcula, from Medieval Latin torcula, from torculum (“wine or olive press”).

b: Darauf kamen die drei Landesflüchtigen an einem Hof vorbei, da saß auf dem Thor der Haushahn und schrie aus Leibeskräften.
然后，三个逃亡者经过一个农庄，大门上坐着一只家养的公鸡，正在拼命地叫。
„Das ist zur Belohnung deiner Dienste“ sagte die Frau Holle und schloß das Thor zu.

Das Thor ward aufgethan, und wie das Mädchen gerade darunter stand, fiel ein gewaltiger Goldregen, und alles Gold blieb an ihm hängen, so daß es über und über davon bedeckt war.
